study.title: Psalm 87 Zion as the city of God and mother of the peoples
study.overview: Psalm 87 celebrates Zion/Jerusalem as a unique place of God's presence and at the same time as a sign of the inclusion of the nations among the Lord's people. The psalm begins with the assertion that Zion's foundation is in the holy mountains and ends with a note of community joy: all the sources of the psalmist are in Zion. Between these two points, the text contrasts the honor of belonging to Zion with the glory of other nations, but shows that the greatest dignity is not in ethnic origin, but in the divine recognition of who belongs to the Lord. In evangelical reading, the psalm points to the centrality of the people of God gathered by the Lord Himself and to the joy of belonging to his city.

outline.title: Zion, founded by God and marked by his glory
outline.explanation: The first verses claim that the city rests on the holy mountains and that the Lord loves it in a special way. Zion is not treated as a simple political center, but as a place associated with the presence and favor of God, which explains the glorious things that are said about him.

outline.title: Nations are registered among the citizens of Zion
outline.explanation: The psalm widens the horizon: peoples previously seen as foreigners - such as Egypt, Babylonia, Philistia, Tyre and Cuxe - appear as a space of origin of people who come to be recognized by God. The emphasis is not on national superiority, but on the fact that the Most High registers who belongs to him.

outline.title: The ultimate joy: all the sources are in you
outline.explanation: The closure is celebrative and probably expressing community joy. The image of the sources suggests that in Zion are the origin, the sustenance and abundance of the life of the people of God.

study.context: The notes received place the psalm in the setting of Jerusalem/Sion as the city of the temple and the divine presence. Some commentators understand the psalm as a song of joy in the face of Zion's prosperity; others relate it to the time when Jerusalem had been rebuilt, which would explain the abrupt and exultant tone. The notes also indicate a typological reading: Zion acts as a figure of the church of the gospel, without this extinguishing the original meaning attached to the holy city.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm affirms the sovereignty of God in the choice of Zion and in the inclusion of nations. Citizenship in God's people depends not only on natural birth, but on the recognition of the Lord, who writes and records his own. This prepares a broad vision of the people of God, in which true glory is to belong to the Lord and receive his identity. In Christian reading, Zion can be understood as a figure of the community of faith, founded by God and sustained by him, with Christ as the main stone; yet this application must be treated as an interpretation and not as the only possible reading of the psalm.

scholarViews.insight: Jerusalem is seen as the city of God in which the nations are treated as citizens, and God holds a record of those who confess him as Lord.
Zion is presented as the type and figure of the gospel church, to which the words of the psalm apply very appropriately.
The expression of those born in Zion is read as an honor to belong to the city of God; in a spiritual sense, it points to be a citizen of heavenly Jerusalem and the son of God by faith in Christ.

questions: What changes in our vision of identity when we understand that belonging to the people of God comes from the recognition of the Lord, and not just human origin?
How does the image of Zion as a place of glory and inclusion confront any religious or nationalistic pride?
What are the sources that in fact support our spiritual life: the city of God or other passing sources?
study.practice: Recognize concretely that true spiritual security comes from the Lord who records his own. This week, pray for people of different backgrounds, remembering that God calls people from many nations and stories to belong to their people. Also examine where you seek sustenance: whether in external advantages, reputation or control, or in God's promises. Long live as one whose primary citizenship is in Zion, that is, in the people of God gathered around him.
study.uncertainty: The psalm is brief and poetic, and some images admit more than one reading. The notes do not provide firm historical details to date the text; therefore, it is not safe to state with absolute certainty whether it was composed at the time of Jerusalem's prosperity or after exile, although both possibilities appear in the aforementioned interpretations. It is also not possible to determine, only with these notes, whether verse 7 should be read primarily as the singer's voice, community, or both.
